INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

On March 23, 2023, the husband and wife
plaintiffs, Alice and George Thmbran, filed a Notice of Civil Claim (NOCC)
against the defendants seeking damages for many civil and
Charter

claims. They filed an Amended Notice of Civil Claim (ANOCC) on April 3, 2023.
The claims arise from an investigation the British Columbia College of Nurses
and Midwives (“the College” or “BCCNM”) conducted of Ms. Thmbran, a Registered
Nurse (“RN”) and Director of Care, following a complaint.

[
2
]

Put at its most basic, the Thmbrans allege that
the College targeted Ms. Thmbran and that the investigation was malicious,
deceitful and fraudulent. They contend that the Inspector, defendant Ms.
Ramanzin, and the College’s legal counsel, defendant Ms. Ohene-Asante, tried to
coerce and threaten Ms. Thmbran.

[
3
]

The plaintiffs assert multiple
Charter

breaches and tort claims including:

a)

Abuse of Rights;

b)

Abuse of Process;

c)

Malicious use of Process;

d)

Civil Conspiracy;

e)

Civil fraud and deceit;

f)

Defamation;

g)

Intentional infliction of Emotional Distress; and

h)

Malfeasance, Misfeasance and Nonfeasance.

[
4
]

In this application the BCCNM defendants,
Cynthia Johansen, Tansey Ramanzin, Aisha Ohene-Asante and the BCCNM Inquiry
Committee, (together “the College”) seek to strike the pleadings pursuant to R.
9-5(1) of the
Supreme Court Civil Rules

or alternatively, have the claims
dismissed pursuant to R. 9-6 on the basis that they raise no genuine issue for
trial. In further alternative, they seek to have the BCCNM Inquiry Committee,
Registrar Johansen and Mr. Thmbran removed as parties pursuant to R. 6-2.

[
5
]

In an overarching response to all of the claims,
the BCCNM defendants argue that the plaintiffs’ claims are barred by the
general statutory immunity conferred on them by the
Disciplinary Authority
Protection Act,
R.S.B.C.1996, c. 98 [
DAPA
] and
s. 24 (1)
of the
Health
Professions Act
, R.S.B.C.1996, c. 183 [
HPA
]. Pursuant to
s. 1
of the

DAPA
, “no liability is incurred by the corporation, or by any body of
the members, or by any official or member of the corporation, or by any person
retained as counsel, solicitor or agent by the corporation for any act or thing
done in the exercise of the disciplinary powers conferred or in doing any act
or thing in preparation for the exercise of those powers,
unless the act or
thing is done maliciously and without reasonable and probable cause
”. Similarly,
s. 24(1) of
HPA
protects a member of a board or a person acting on
behalf of or under the direction of a board or college from legal action on the
basis of their performance or exercise of any power under the Act
done in
good faith
. I emphasise the preceding phrases to illustrate that the key to
statutory immunity as per these provisions is lack of malice or lack of good
faith. The plaintiffs submit that the defendants acted with malice, without
reasonable and probable cause, and in bad faith.

[
6
]

In further overarching response, the BCCNM
defendants contend that the plaintiffs have failed to clearly plead the
material facts necessary to support each of their distinct claims or delineate with
sufficient clarity which facts relate to which cause of action or to which
defendant with respect to each of their claims.

[
7
]

In assessing the sufficiency of the plaintiffs’
pleadings, I am mindful that they are representing themselves, with no legal
training, and that English is not their first language. Accordingly, I will
give the plaintiffs a degree of leeway to ensure that they are provided with
fair access to justice and equal treatment by the court.

[
8
]

Defendant, His Majesty the King in Right of the
Province of British Columbia (Ministry of Health) (“the Province”) seeks to
strike claims against it pursuant to R. 9-5 (1)(a) and (b) by arguing that
there is no basis for statutory or vicarious liability on the part of the
Province.

[
9
]

In these reasons for judgment, for ease of
reference, I will refer to the plaintiffs as Alice and George. I mean no
disrespect by doing so.

[
10
]

I note that on November 24, 2022, the BC Legislative Assembly passed
the
Health Professions and Occupations Act,
S.B.C. 2022, c. 43; however,
as of writing these reasons for judgment, it has not come into force. Accordingly,
all reference to the legislation that governs health professionals and
regulatory colleges will be to the
HPA
as it was when applied to the
matters below.

BACKGROUND

[
11
]

In order to consider whether there is merit to the plaintiff’s
claims I must review the background facts in detail.

The Parties

[
12
]

The regulatory body for the professions of nursing, psychiatric
nursing, practical nursing and midwifery amalgamated twice during the course of
this dispute. For ease of reference, I will use BCCNM and/or College in these
reasons for judgment. The College is responsible for carrying out the objects
of the
HPA
, including the duty to serve and protect the public and the responsibility
to deal with the discipline of College registrants.

[
13
]

The defendant Cynthia
Johansen

is the Registrar and CEO of the College (the “Registrar”).

[
14
]

Tansy Ramanzin (the “Inspector”) is the professional review
consultant officer of the College. She was appointed as an inspector under
s.
27(1)
of the
HPA
. She investigated the complaint against the plaintiff,
Alice.

[
15
]

Aisha Ohene-Asante is the legal counsel for the College who dealt
with the complaint against Alice.

[
16
]

The BCCNM Inquiry Committee (the “Inquiry Committee”) is established
under
s. 19(1)
(t) of the
HPA
. It has statutory decision-making authority
under the
HPA
. Its duty is to protect the public and to act in the
public interest.

[
17
]

The Ministry of Health of the government of British Columbia
delegated authority to the College under the
HPA
to govern the nursing
profession in the province.

[
18
]

From October 2016 to February 2018, Alice was a registered nurse
(“RN”) and the Director of Care (“DOC”) at Maple Ridge Seniors Village (the “Facility”).
As DOC, Alice supervised a team of RNs, licenced practical nurses (“LPN”) and
resident care aides (“RCA”). From the evidence filed on this application, Alice
was highly regarded for her work. In fact, on January 10, 2018, Alice was asked
to be the acting General Manager (GM) as well as DOC, when the former GM left
abruptly.

[
19
]

On January 28, 2018, an LPN documented a report by resident—Ms. C—that
another resident—Mr. H—had acted toward her in a sexually inappropriate manner on
two occasions. Both incidents were unwitnessed.

[
20
]

The next day, January 29, 2018, a number of things happened. Alice
was contacted by a family member of Ms. C who notified her of the incidents. Alice
immediately submitted the necessary report and created a behaviour care/action
plan, including one-on-one monitoring of Mr. H every 30 minutes. Alice
communicated with the interdisciplinary team and both of the residents’ decision-makers.
A family member of Ms. C reported the incidents to the police. When police
attended the Facility that same day the action plan was already being followed.
Alice reported the incident to her supervisor, the Regional Director of
Operations of Retirement Concepts, and advised her of her plan. The Regional
Director approved Alice’s plan.

[
21
]

On February 5, 2018, Alice was injured on the job (in an unrelated
incident) and was on medical leave until January 2020. While on leave, Alice
lodged an unrelated human rights complaint through the BC Human Rights Tribunal
(BCHRT) against her employer for bullying and harassment.

The Blatta Complaint

[
22
]

In early June 2019, again while Alice was on leave (and had been for
approximately 16 months), Lynn Blatta, a RCA at the Facility, placed a
complaint with the College against Alice alleging inaction and cover-up of
sexual assaults and “rape” (Ms. Blatta’s term) perpetrated by Mr. H on
vulnerable female residents from June 2016 to February 2018. Ms. Blatta also named
another nurse, Kanika Ghosh and a LPN, Laura Rempel in her complaint.

[
23
]

To Inspector Ramanzin, Ms. Blatta reported that on
January 30,
2018,
she “popped her head into Ms. M’s room” (another resident) and saw
Mr. H on top of Ms. M who was laying on her back on her bed. Ms. Blatta described
that
Mr. H had his pants down. His penis was erect. Mr. H had one of his
knees on Ms. M’s chest and was hitting Ms. M in the face with his penis. He
then shoved his penis into Ms. M’s mouth. Ms. M was gurgling and choking and
looked scared.
Ms. Blatta reported that she immediately pulled the call
bell for help and pushed Mr. H off Ms. M. In support of her allegation, Ms.
Blatta provided the Inspector with a calendar on which she had written in the
January 30, 2018 space, “H raped Ms. M”. The evidence does not indicate when
Ms. Blatta made this notation.

[
24
]

Ms. Blatta told the Inspector that Mr. H was “in his 80s”, who
“apparently had dementia” and had an “intentful (sic) component to his
behaviour”. According to Alice, Mr. H was 93 years old at the time of the alleged
incident, needed a walker for mobility, was at high risk for falls and required
assistance with care. He suffered from many diagnoses including dementia and a
fractured hip. Though he spoke English, it was not his first language.

[
25
]

I emphasise the date and some details of the complaint as the dates
and substance of the allegations change as the investigation proceeds. That is
a significant aspect of Alice’s complaint.

[
26
]

The entry by Ms. Blatta on her personal calendar was the only record
of an incident on January 30, 2018. There was no notation of this incident in the
January 30, 2018 nursing logs. In fact, the documentation was that after the 30-minute
reviews were implemented by Alice on January 29, 2018, no further inappropriate
behaviour occurred.

[
27
]

In addition to the January 30 incident, Ms. Blatta told the Inspector
that on February 15, 2018,
she
saw Mr. H forcing Ms. M into his room. Ms.
Blatta reported that
she
intervened and kept Ms. M safe. Inspector
Ramanzin documented that it was in fact Harjit, a RCA, that witnessed Mr. H trying
to direct Ms. M into his room and intervened, not Ms. Blatta.

[
28
]

Ms. Blatta reported the February incident to police. Police
investigated and took no action against Mr. H.

[
29
]

Ms. Blatta told the Inspector that the police officer who
investigated her complaint “thought Alice was guilty of criminal negligence”.
The RCMP confirmed to Alice that at no time did police ever suspect or accuse her
of criminal negligence.

BCCNM Inquiry Committee Orders an
Investigation

[
30
]

On June 13, 2019, the Inquiry Committee ordered an investigation
into the Blatta complaint.

[
31
]

Despite the fact that she was on medical leave,
the Inquiry Committee immediately issued an interim undertaking against Alice
restricting her from working anywhere other than the Facility. As a result,
when Alice did return to work, it was to the Facility.

[
32
]

According to Alice, she felt that she had to
withdraw her BCHRT complaint to ease the tension at work. Nonetheless, Alice
states that she was subjected to further harassment at the Facility.

[
33
]

Although the defendants maintain that Alice
could have applied to have the undertaking changed, I disagree that the process
was that simple. The undertaking states as follows:

2. Despite the
above, I understand that if, after agreeing to this Undertaking, I no longer
wish to abide by the terms of the Undertaking, I must immediately advise BCCNP
of my desire to be released from the Undertaking. I understand that the terms
will not be removed until the investigative file has been reviewed in light of
the Inquiry Committee's powers to take extraordinary action under section 35 of
the Act to impose conditions or limits on - or a suspension of - registration
during the course of investigation. This review will not take more than 30
days.

[
34
]

According to the evidence, the next time that the Inquiry Committee
met was on March 17, 2020, nine months after the first meeting. At this meeting,
the Inquiry Committee assessed the investigation as “being adequate” and found on
the evidence provided by the Inspector, that Alice’s conduct was “not
satisfactory”.

Consent Order #1

[
35
]

At the March 17, 2021 meeting, the Inquiry Committee concluded that
the appropriate remedy was for Alice to
voluntarily relinquish her
registration
with the College
and not be permitted to apply for reinstatement
for three years
. I emphasize the penalty as what the Inquiry Committee concluded
was appropriate remedial action changed drastically over the following nine months.

[
36
]

According to the meeting minutes the factual basis for this decision
included the following:

a)

“On
January 10
,
the Complainant [Ms. Blatta] discovered

Mr. H pinning Ms. M to
a
bed
with his knee
. He had
pulled down
his pants
.
The Complainant, the only witness
, asserts that
Mr. H
rubbed and slapped his penis around Ms. M's mouth
, though this is not
explicitly documented in the record or behavioural log”.

I pause to note
that the now January 10 (instead of January 30 as reported by Ms. Blatta)
incident took place on an unspecified bed rather than Ms. M’s bed as described
by Ms. Blatta.

b)

“The RN on duty (RN Ghosh) documented that
she discussed the
matter with [Alice]
, who directed that the physician be notified…”

I again pause to
note that RN Ghosh only recorded “DOC aware of incident”, not that she notified
Alice or discussed the matter with her. It was a key point that needed to be
clarified as RN Ghosh’s entry followed the entry of LPN Jayakody—the person
that actually witnessed the event and wrote that she would be following up with
the DOC. RN Ghosh was never interviewed by the Inspector. Neither was Alice.

c)

“Despite this, and despite confirmatory and contemporaneous
documentation in the medicolegal record, [Alice] denies knowing about the
incident. The Inquiry Committee acknowledged the conflict in evidence and in
their screening of the evidence, was of the opinion that the record supported
that [Alice] was aware of the three incidents. As a result, the Inquiry Committee
was concerned about [Alice’s] ethics, veracity, accountability and
governability.”

d)

“[RN Ghosh] asserted that [Alice] said she would submit an external
incident report. No Incident Report was submitted, contrary to regulation.”

RN Ghosh’s entry
does not say that Alice told her that she would submit an incident report. And
as noted above, RN Ghosh was not interviewed.

e)

“Mr. H’s behaviour continued to escalate”. He kissed Ms. M on the
lips on January 14 and groped the breasts and genital areas of two other female
residents on January 28.”

f)

“
Once police and Licencing became involved,
[Alice] took action
. She submitted an Incident Report and created an Action
Plan.”

g)

“Despite stating that q 30 minute monitoring would occur post the
January 28 assaults, q 30 minute behavioural log forms were not put into place
until February 16, 2018, after police visited and confirmed the safety planning
was not being done. The Registrant was on leave at that time but did not
ensure, prior to going on leave on February 6, that the monitoring sheets were
being completed. The Registrant said she did not believe that 1:1 monitoring
was required prior to 1700h, because Mr. H went to recreational activities and
recreational staff had no concerns. Review of the patient record shows that
sexual assaults happened during day time hours (before 1700h). The Registrant
would not have known as she admitted that she did not review Mr. H's record.
She felt that she could create an action plan and then conduct a follow up
investigation at a later date; it was not a priority.
Given this
decision-making, the Committee questions the ability of [Alice] to competently
prioritize patient safety
.”

[
37
]

As noted above, the Inquiry Committee offered to resolve the matter
through a consent order. Alice was asked to agree that the facts as outlined
above, were true and accurate and to
agree to a cancellation of her nursing
registration and to not apply for reinstatement for at least three years
.
According to the Consent Order, this penalty was “necessary to ensure public
safety and future adherence to the professional standards established or
otherwise expected by BCCNP.” I will refer to this as CO #1.

[
38
]

The facts that Alice was required to admit were
set out in CO#1. Of note, the main incident, now dated January 10 had changed
again in CO#1 to be on Mr. H’s bed instead of Ms. M’s as reported by Ms. Blatta
or “a bed” as per the meeting minutes, as follows:

On January 10,
2018, Mr. H was found with Ms. M
on his bed
. The complainant [Ms.
Blatta], who witnessed the incident, said on interview (sic) with BCCNP that
Mr. H had his pants down and removed his erect penis from his underwear. He had
pinned Ms. M to the bed with his knee and was rubbing his penis around her face
and mouth. She disclosed this incident to a friend shortly thereafter. The
behaviour log entry (written by [Ms. Blatta
]
and associated nursing
progress note (written by a
non-witness LPN
), do not particularize Mr.
H’s actions but did note that
he had Ms. M on his bed and had pulled down
his pants
…

[
39
]

This account of the January 10 incident is
inaccurate. The progress note was authored by the person that actually saw the
incident, LPN Jayakody, who described the incident much differently than the Inspector
did to the Inquiry Committee or in CO#1:

RCA called for help.
Writer
went to
see, and found female resident lying down
on resident’s bed

and
resident was pulling his pants down and only with underwear
;
writer able
to separate both residents and redirect the female resident away from the room
;
resident was upset about the separation and states that she was his girlfriend
and ask the writer what do you care about it; so writer explain that she was
not her girlfriend or wife and came out from resident’s room; RN aware about
the incident; family need to be informed.
Will F/U with DOC
and further
direction.

[Emphasis added.]

[
40
]

LPN Jayakody described the RCA that called for help as Filipina. Ms.
Blatta is Caucasian.

[
41
]

For unspecified reasons, the Inspector chose Ms. Blatta’s
description of the incident, changing the date and location. That was an
apparent attempt to fit with the progress notes kept at the Facility. However,
the Inspector evidently failed to check the work schedule and missed a key
issue: Ms. Blatta was not working on January 10, 2018.

[
42
]

Alice’s knowledge of the January 10, 2018 incident was crucial to
the College’s case. In a follow-up, the Inspector asked LPN Jayakody what he
meant when he recorded that he would follow up. LPN Jayakody’s response was
less than clear. According to the Inspector’s notes, he responded that he had
“generally meant the management team which included the RN, Director of Care and
General manager”. His interview was based on what he said he remembered from a
time that was “long ago”. He said there were two ways to submit an incident
report—online and by paper. The paper reports were “always submitted”, usually
they were slid under the Director of Care’s door. Online reports had to be
reviewed via a web portal by the morning RN or Director of Care. He does not
know why [Alice] said, “there was no incident reports."

[
43
]

Alice refused to enter into CO#1. In her email to
the Inspector dated June 29, 2020, Alice advised the Inspector of the reasons
for doing so as follows:

Hereby, I am notifying BCCNP of my strong
disapproval of the decision of the Inquiry Committee. The Facts on the consent
agreement are not based on evidences rather BCCNP misrepresented information on
each fact to falsely accuse me of professional misconduct and inaction. BCCNP
has completely disregarded evidence based facts and deliberately provided
misleading information on the consent agreement. Hence, Failed to ensure
procedural fairness.

It is my understanding that, BCCNP is
Scapegoating me to protect BCNU members. Henceforth, as a health professional
regulatory board BCCNP failed to abide by its public protection mandate by
failing to take action against the registrants who are actually guilty of their
action/inaction even after becoming aware of it. BCCNP is misusing the
regulatory authority to punish/penalize me rather than ensuring public safety.

I am really dismayed by the mistreatment I
received from BCCNP. I never expected this kind of targeted and outrageous
action from the nursing regulator to punish/penalize an innocent in order to
protect and cover up for multiple registrants who are members of BCNU. I feel
total injustice, The entire inquiry process (investigation stage) was
deliberated in bad faith.

Though, I find it difficult to stand up
against such a powerful organization like BCCNP, I find it very important to
fight for my rights and protect my integrity as a person.

Hence I decline
to sign the consent agreement.

[
44
]

Alice’s mental state declined significantly after she received the
College’s resolution offer. In an April 20, 2020 letter, Alice’s treating psychiatrist,
Dr. Anwar stated that Alice suffered a setback when she received CO#1 and was
“in acute distress”. She had been starting to improve but this offer caused her
to deteriorate. The doctor noted that “Alice has poor distress tolerance,
catastrophic thinking and tends to jumps (sic) to conclusions. She tends to
have intense dysphoria secondary to stress and keeps dipping back into
depressed state.” In a follow-up letter, the psychiatrist notes that Alice
condition had worsened due to the letter from the College seeking the
revocation of her licence. She was not getting out of bed and was not talking.
She was eating little. She expressed hopelessness. The doctor suggested
hospitalization. The doctor’s letter dated April 27, 2020, reported that
Alice’s state was slowly starting to improve.

Citation Issued

[
45
]

On July 15, 2020, the Inspector advised Alice via e-mail that because
she refused to sign CO#1, “the Inquiry Committee directed issuance of a
citation for a hearing of the BCCNP Discipline Committee and that jurisdiction
of the process has now been assumed by the BCCNP Legal Team who will be in
touch in due course.” That direction was made on July 14, 2020.

[
46
]

The Citation issued September 9, 2020 by
Registrar/CEO Cynthia Johansen sets out that the purpose of the hearing is to
inquire into Alice’s conduct as follows:

1.

On multiple occasions between October 24, 2016
to February 6, 2018 you failed to take steps to protect female residents under
your care from non-consensual sexual behaviour, including sexual abuse, from a
male co-resident, when you knew or ought to have known the male co-resident was
behaving in a sexually inappropriate manner, contrary to one or more of the
following Professional Standards and/or Practice Standards: the
Responsibility
and Accountability
Professional Standard, the
Client- Focused Provision
of Service
Professional Standard, the
Ethical Practice
Professional
Standard, and the
Documentation Practice
Standard.

This conduct also constitutes unprofessional conduct, or breach of
the Act or bylaws, under s.39 (1) of the Act.

2.

On multiple occasions between October 24, 2016
to February 6, 2018 you failed in your duty to report the sexual abuse of
female residents by a male co-resident, contrary to one or more of the
following Professional Standards and/or Practice Standards: the
Responsibility
and Accountability
Professional Standard, the
Client-Focused Provision
of Service
Professional Standard, the
Ethical Practice
Professional
Standard.

This conduct also
constitutes unprofessional conduct, or breach of the Act or bylaws, under s.39
(1) of the Act.

[
47
]

In an email to legal counsel on November 19, 2020, Alice sought
clarification of the allegations and the process and expressed her desire to go
to hearing as well as her hope that she will get a fair hearing.

Consent Order #2

[
48
]

Despite Alice’s clear wish to go to hearing to clear her name, on
November 20, 2020, the College attempted to resolve this disciplinary matter
again via a new consent order. There is no evidence as to what prompted this
offer.

[
49
]

Consent Order #2 (CO#2) begins that Ms. Blatta alleges that between
June
2016 and April 2018,
Alice was aware that vulnerable female residents were
being sexually assaulted by a male resident and that she took no action to
protect them. I emphasize the dates of the allegation. Alice did not work at
the facility for at least seven months of the period of her alleged wrongdoing.

[
50
]

In CO#2 the January 10 incident changed again. This time the Inspector
(who according to the evidence is responsible for drafting the consent orders)
described the incident as “
on or about
January 10, 2018, Mr. H was found
with Female resident #1 in his room and
he had pulled down his pants to
expose his penis
.” I pause to note that there is no evidence of this. This
is a markedly toned-down version of the Blatta allegations.

[
51
]

In CO#2 the College was seeking a significantly shorter suspension: 6-months.

[
52
]

In the covering letter to Alice attaching CO#2, legal counsel
Asante-Ohene
notes that the September 9, 2020 citation
sets out the allegations BCCNM intends to prove at the Disciplinary Hearing
scheduled to begin on January 25, 2021. She further notes that the citation
will be posted on the BCCNM website shortly. Ms.
Asante-Ohene

then states that she encloses a draft consent order for Alice’s
consideration and that while it is open to negotiation she anticipates “that
the Inquiry Committee will not approve a consent resolution at this point
without significant admissions on your part”.

[
53
]

Legal counsel Asante-Ohene closes by stating that if the College is
successful in proving the allegations at hearing “then it will be a more
serious penalty than set out in the Consent Order and may include submissions
that your registration be cancelled. In addition, there may be a financial
penalty and costs award made against you”. Ms. Asante-Ohene provides examples
of cost awards made in other cases that range from $12,500 to $36,000.

[
54

]

ISSUES

[
70
]

The issues are whether any or all of the claims should be struck
against any or all of the defendants.

[
71
]

I will address each claim in turn but first, I will outline the
applicable law.

THE LAW

Rule
9-5

[
72
]

Rule 9-5 of the
Supreme Court Civil Rules
,
B.C. Reg. 168/2009 governs applications to strike. It reads as follows:

(1)
At any stage of a proceeding, the court may order to be struck out
or amended the whole or any part of a pleading, petition or other document on
the ground that

(a)
it discloses
no reasonable claim or defence, as the case may be,

(b)
it is
unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c)
it may
prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing of the proceeding, or

(d)
it is
otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court
may pronounce judgment or order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and
may order the costs of the application to be paid as special costs.

[
73
]

Although the subsections address different concerns, there is
overlap between them. For example, a pleading may disclose no cause of action
contrary to Rule 9-5(1)(a) and also be unnecessary and vexatious contrary to
Rule 9-5(1)(b):
Sahyoun v. Ho
,
2015 BCSC 392
at para.
61
.

[
74
]

Rule 9-5(1)(a) of the
Supreme Court

Civil Rules

provides that the court may strike the whole or any part of a proceeding on the
grounds that it discloses no reasonable claim.

[
75
]

A claim will be struck if it is plain and obvious, assuming the
facts pleaded to be true, that the pleading discloses no reasonable cause of
action:
Knight v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd.
,
2011 SCC 42
at para.
17
.
The court must read the plaintiff’s pleadings as generously towards the
plaintiffs as possible:
Knight
at para.
17
.

[
76
]

Rule 9-5 is an attack on pleadings on the basis that the claim as
pleaded or as it may reasonably be amended cannot succeed as a matter of law.
In assessing an application under Rule 9-5 the court is confined to a
consideration of the pleading. Evidence is not to be considered:
Drummond v.
Moore
,
2012 BCSC 496
at paras.
16-23
.

[
77
]

In terms of particularization of claims, the threshold is low to
support a plaintiff’s claim prior to discovery. It has been described as “some
evidence even if very little”:
Proconic Electronics Limited and Far East
United Electronics Ltd. v. Wong et al
., (1985)
1985 CanLII 253 (BC SC)
, 67 B.C.L.R. 237 at p. 241 as
followed in
Tour-Mate Technologies Corp. v. Syntronix Systems Ltd
.,

1993 CanLII 2250 (BC SC)
, [1993] B.C.J. No. 599 at para.
15
. The plaintiff must be able to explore its
claim without having its hands tied, particularly when some required
information might be in the hands of yet-to-be discovered defendants:
Cambie
Forming Ltd
.
v. Accuform Construction Ltd.
,
2016 BCSC 266
at paras.

34-43
. Claims should not be struck out under s. 9-5(1)(a)
if the statement as it stands,
or as it may be amended
, discloses a
cause of action: see
Carhoun & Sons Enterprises Ltd. v. Canada
(Attorney General),
2015 BCCA 163
at para.
133
.

[
78
]

The rule that material facts in a notice of civil claim must be
assumed to be true does not mean that allegations based on assumptions and
speculation must be taken as true. Rather, such allegations must be subjected
to a skeptical analysis in order to determine their true character:
Young v.
Borzoni et al
,
2007 BCCA 16
at paras.
25-32
.

[
79
]

The test for striking a pleading under Rule
9-5(1)(b) was summarised by Fisher, J., as she then was, in
Willow v. Chong
,

2013 BCSC 1083
at para.
20
:

Under Rule
9-5(1)(b), a pleading is unnecessary or vexatious if it does not go to
establishing the plaintiff’s cause of action,
if it does not advance any
claim known in law, where it is obvious that an action cannot succeed, or where
it would serve no useful purpose and would be a waste of the court’s time and
public resources:
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v Canadian Jewish
Congress
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] BCJ No. 2160 (SC);
Skender v Farley
,
2007 BCCA
629
. If a pleading is so confusing that it is difficult to understand what is
pleaded, it may also be unnecessary, frivolous or vexatious. An application
under this sub-rule may be supported by evidence.

[Emphasis
added.]

[
80
]

Abuse of process under Rule 9-5(1)(d) is a flexible doctrine that
allows the court to prevent a claim from proceeding where to do so would
violate principles of judicial economy, finality and the integrity of the
administration of justice:
Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E. Local 79,

2003 SCC
63
at paras.
35-37
.

Rule 9-6

[
81
]

Rule 9-6, the summary
judgment rule, is employed to prevent claims or defences that have no chance of
success from proceeding to trial. It reads in relevant part as follows:

(4)        In
an action, an answering party may, after serving a responding pleading on a
claiming party, apply under this rule for judgment dismissing all or part of a
claim in the claiming party's originating pleading.

(5)        On
hearing an application under subrule (2) or (4), the court,

(a)   if
satisfied that there is no genuine issue for trial with respect to a claim or
defence, must pronounce judgment or dismiss the claim accordingly,

….

and

(d)   may make any other order it considers will further
the object of these
Supreme Court Civil Rules
.

[
82
]

The onus
is on the party seeking the summary dismissal to prove that there is no genuine
issue for trial. If the defendant is able to meet this high bar, the burden
shifts to the plaintiff to refute or counter the defendant’s evidence:
Canada
v. Lameman
,
2008 SCC 14
at paras.
10 and 11
.

[
83
]

A
challenge under R. 9-6 is based on a limited review of the evidence.

Rule 6-2

[
84
]

Rule 6-2(7)(a) permits the court to order that a person cease to be
a party if that person is not, or has ceased to be, a proper or necessary party.

ANALYSIS OF PLAINTIFFS’ CLAIMS

[
85
]

With the background facts and law in mind, I now turn to address the
applications. I will consider the merits of each of the alleged torts in turn
then I will consider the
Charter
breaches together.

Abuse of Rights

[
86
]

There is no tort of abuse of rights. This claim is struck pursuant
to Rule 9-5(1)(a).

Abuse of Process and Malicious Use
of Process

[
87
]

I will address these torts separately

Abuse of Process

[
88
]

In order to establish the tort of abuse of process the plaintiff
must establish the following elements:

(i)

A collateral and improper purpose;

(ii)

An overt act in furtherance of the collateral and improper purpose;
and,

(iii)

Resulting loss.

See Oei v. Hui
,
2020 BCCA 214

[
89
]

The proceedings in issue were administrative and did not involve a court
process. As such there is no reasonable chance of success to a claim for abuse
of process.

[
90
]

I agree with the defendants that it appears that the plaintiffs are
confusing the tort of abuse of process with procedural fairness. Procedural
fairness is the subject of judicial review, not an action for damages.

[
91
]

Our Court of Appeal in
The College of Physicians and Surgeons of
British Columbia v. The Health Professions Review Board,

2022 BCCA 10
; has
said that an “investigation and disposition by the inquiry committee is an
exercise of a statutory power amenable to review under the
Judicial
Review Procedure Act” (
at

para. 198). Consistent with this, the
BCCNM defendants have said in their Notice of Application at para. 33 that “if
Alice is dissatisfied with the content of the Letter of Expectations, it
remains open to her to apply to the court for Judicial Review of the
disposition of the Complaint against her.”

[
92
]

I find that there is basis for Alice to argue on Judicial Review that
the apparent arbitrariness of the process, the ever-changing “facts” and dates,
and the significantly different consent orders offered with the significantly
different penalties on the same facts all point to procedural unfairness (and
perhaps bad faith). It is further open to Alice to argue that the final
resolution was procedurally unfair (and perhaps in bad faith) as it robbed
Alice of proper notice, the opportunity, to clear her name (which the college
knew she wanted), made final findings of “fact” that the College knew she
refuted and took away from her any avenue of review or appeal.

[
93
]

The claim for abuse of process is struck
pursuant to Rule 9-5(1)(a) as it discloses no reasonable claim.

[
94
]

I grant leave to the plaintiffs to amend the proceedings to bring a petition
for Judicial Review if they see fit and extend time for doing so until May 15,
2024.

Malicious Use of Process
(Malicious Prosecution)

[
95
]

There is no tort of malicious use of process. The tort of malicious
prosecution – not malicious use of process – is most aligned with their
pleadings. Given that the plaintiffs are not legally trained, I am satisfied on
this application to strike, that I may generously construe the plaintiff’s
claim as the tort of malicious prosecution and not “malicious use of process.”

[
96
]

The plaintiffs allege that the defendants knew that there were no
reasonable and probable grounds for the citation, the decisions of the Inquiry
Committee were based on misstatements of fact provided by the Inspector, and
the Inquiry Committee denied Alice of a hearing on its merits, which caused her
emotional distress and left a permanent black mark on her nursing employment
record.

[
97
]

In a trilogy of cases from the Supreme Court of Canada, four
elements of malicious prosecution in
criminal proceedings
were defined
in
Nelles v. Ontario
,
1989 CanLII 77 (SCC)
, [1989] 2 SCR 170;
Proulx c Quebec (procureur
général),
2001 SCC 66
, and
Miazga v. Kvello Estate
,
2009 SCC 51
as:

(i)

the defendant initiated or is actively
instrumental in setting the proceedings in motion;

(ii)

the proceedings were terminated in favour of the plaintiff;

(iii)

the absence of reasonable and probable cause; and

(iv)

malice, or a primary purpose other than that of carrying the law
into effect.

[
98
]

To date, the judiciary has been cautious in applying liability for
malicious prosecution outside of criminal proceedings and upon self-regulatory
bodies. In
New Brunswick Real Estate Association v. Estabrooks
,
2014
NBCA 48
, leave to appeal to SCC ref’d, [2014] SCCA No 404, the majority of the
New Brunswick Court of Appeal held that “an action for malicious prosecution
cannot lie against a provincial self-regulating disciplinary body for the
actions taken by members of its disciplinary committee in the court of their
duties.” (
Estabrooks
at para.
58
). However, if that action were
available, the Court reasoned that the claim would ultimately fail on
application of the four elements of the tort. In particular, there were
challenges in establishing that a party had initiated or was actively
instrumental in setting the proceedings in motion given the interplay of the statutory
obligation to investigate complaints. Additionally, a spiteful demeanor by the
Registrar was not sufficient to meet the high threshold of the fourth element:
malice. In dissent, B. Richard Bell J.A. would have found the tort applicable
by stating at para. 83,

“…I would
observe that if the state is prepared to grant a legislative mandate to
professional bodies to discipline their members, up to and including
prohibiting them from practicing in their field, those bodies should be
expected to always act in good faith with proper motives and to refrain from
maliciously prosecuting one of their own.”

[
99
]

In
Bahadar v. Real Estate Council of Alberta (RECA)
,
2021
ABQB 395
at para.
34
, the Alberta Court of King’s Bench was of the view that
Estabrooks

does not definitively settle the law on this matter and upheld a lower court decision
not to strike a claim for malicious prosecution against a self-regulatory body.
In that case, Mr. Bahadar made allegations similar to the present case: that
the regulator had proceeded with disciplinary actions despite knowing that they
had no case, based their actions on false evidence, and concealed relevant
facts.

[
100
]

For the purpose of this striking application, I
need only be satisfied that there are some particulars to show improper motive
or purpose: see
Bahadar
at para.
73
.  I am so satisfied.

[
101
]

I find that there is evidence on all of the factors defined in
Nelles

above:

a)

The defendants initiated the disciplinary proceedings;

b)

The proceedings were resolved by the defendants in favour of Alice;

c)

There is a factual basis (exemplified by the ever-changing facts and
arguably arbitrary attempts to resolve the proceedings) to support the
contention that there was an absence of reasonable and probable cause;

d)

There are inferences within the evidence to suggest that some or all
of the defendants proceeded for a purpose other than to carry out their
disciplinary process, including the ever-changing factual basis, the arguably
arbitrary offers to resolve and the final decision to resolve the proceedings
in a way that leaves Alice with no avenue of appeal.

[
102
]

Based on the evidence before me, as outlined above, I am satisfied that
the claim of malicious prosecution presents a genuine issue for trial. It is
not plain and obvious that the claim will fail. I strike the claim for
malicious use of process pursuant to Rule 9-5(1)(a) and grant leave to the
plaintiffs to amend their pleadings to bring a claim for malicious prosecution.

Civil Conspiracy

[
103
]

In order to succeed on a claim of civil conspiracy the following
elements must be proved:

1.
an agreement between two or more persons;

2.
concerted action taken pursuant to the agreement;

3.
one of the following:

(i) if the action is lawful, there must be evidence that the conspirators
intended to cause damage to the plaintiff;

(ii)
if the action is unlawful, there must at least be evidence that the
conspirators knew or ought to have known that their action would injure the
plaintiff (i.e., constructive intent);

4.
actual damage suffered by the plaintiff.

See
H.M.B. Holdings Limited v. Replay Resorts Inc.,
2021
BCCA 142
at para.
66
.

[
104
]

There are no material facts to support this claim. Accordingly, it
has no prospect of success and must be struck pursuant to Rule 9-5(1)(a).

Civil Fraud or Deceit

[
105
]

In order to establish civil fraud or deceit, the plaintiffs must
prove: (1) that the defendant made a false statement or representation; (2) some
level of knowledge of the falsehood of the representation on the part of the
defendant (whether through knowledge or recklessness); (3) the false
representation caused the plaintiff to act; and (4) the plaintiff’s actions
resulted in a loss. Reliance on the defendant’s false representation is a
necessary element of this tort. See
Bruno Appliance and Furniture Inc. v.
Hryniak
,
2014 SCC 8
at para.
21
.

[
106
]

Although there is some basis for an argument that the College’s
advice to the plaintiffs that the matter was going to Disciplinary Hearing was
false, and the College knew it was false, as the file was never transferred
from the Inquiry Committee to the Discipline Committee, there is no evidence of
the third and fourth elements.

[
107
]

As such I find that this claim has no reasonable prospect of success
and must be struck pursuant to Rule 9-5(1)(a).

Defamation

[
108
]

Words that tend to lower the plaintiff’s reputation in the eyes of a
reasonable person are defamatory.

[
109
]

In order to succeed in an action for defamation, the plaintiff must
prove: 1) that the impugned words were defamatory; 2) that they referred to the
plaintiff; and 3) that they were published, meaning that they were communicated
to at least one other person. If the plaintiff establishes these elements, the
fact that the statements are false and that they caused damage are presumed and
the onus shifts to the defendant to advance a defence in order to escape
liability. As defamation is a tort of strict liability, it is unnecessary to
prove that the defendant intended to cause harm. See
Weaver v. Corcoran
,

2017 BCCA 160
at para.
70
.

[
110
]

The plaintiffs’ defamation claim is based on BCCMN’s publication of
the citation when it never intended to proceed to a Disciplinary Hearing. As
mentioned above, a citation is issued and published only if the Inquiry
Committee determines that the complaint will proceed to a Disciplinary Hearing.
In this case, the Inquiry Committee advised Alice that the matter was going to Disciplinary
Hearing, issued and published the citation, but never transferred the file to
the Discipline Committee. Then shortly before the hearing date the Inquiry
Committee decided to “resolve” the complaint by way of a Letter of Expectation.
I agree with the plaintiffs that this evidence is consistent with the BCCNM
never intending to go to Disciplinary Hearing.

[
111
]

The BCCNM defendants argue that the plaintiffs have failed to
clearly plead what specific words in the published citation are false, which
they contend is an essential component of this cause of action. They further
argue that the publication was shielded by absolute or qualified privilege.

[
112
]

Alice takes the position that all of the allegations in the Citation
against her are false. She maintained that position and voiced her wish to
prove the allegations false throughout her dealings with the College. It is her
position that the publication of these false allegations lowered her reputation
with her colleagues.

[
113
]

I am unable to say that this claim has no reasonable prospect of
success or that it is shielded by any form of privilege. I do however agree with
the defendants that the pleadings must be clarified to specify which words in
the publication the plaintiffs claim to be defamatory. As the plaintiffs are
representing themselves and English is not their first language, I give them
some latitude when assessing the sufficiency of their pleadings. I grant leave
to the plaintiffs to amend their pleadings to clarify exactly what words they
say are defamatory.

Intentional Infliction of
Emotional Distress

[
114
]

To establish a cause of action for intentional infliction of
emotional distress, a plaintiff must demonstrate conduct that is (1) flagrant
and extreme, (2) plainly calculated to produce harm, and which (3) results in
visible and provable illness:
Lu v. Shen
,
2020 BCSC 490
at para.
257
.

[
115
]

I am satisfied that there is a credible basis for showing that the
College took actions that were plainly calculated to produce harm to Alice.
There are some facts that could be taken as flagrant and extreme. There is also
some evidence to prove that Alice suffered a visible and provable illness
caused by those actions. While the College argues that Alice was already
suffering from a mental illness due to her BCHRT claim, there is evidence which
proves that her condition worsened as a result of this.

[
116
]

I am unable to find that there is no reasonable prospect of success
to this claim.

Misfeasance, Malfeasance, and Nonfeasance

[
117
]

Misfeasance and malfeasance are often used
interchangeably. They are positive acts by public officials committed with a
corrupt, dishonest or oppressive intent. Nonfeasance concerns the neglect of
official duties and does not require a specific intent or
mens rea (R. v.
Boulanger
,
2006 SCC 32
at para.
19
). Based on this distinction, it appears
most useful to focus on misfeasance.

[
118
]

Misfeasance in public office has been described
by our Court of Appeal as “among the most egregious of tortious misconduct”:
J.P.
v. British Columbia (Children and Family Development)
,
2017 BCCA 308
(“
J.P
.”)
at para.
320
.

[
119
]

The court in
J.P.
provides the rationale behind the tort and the
elements required to prove it as follows:

[321]

The tort is based on the
premise that those who hold public office may not exercise their power in a
deliberate and unlawful manner for the ulterior or improper purpose of harming
a member of the public. The rationale for the tort was articulated by Lord
Steyn in
Three Rivers

D.C. v. Bank of England,
[2000]
W.L.R. 1220 at 1230 (U.K.H.L.): “… in a legal system based on the rule of law
executive or administrative power ‘may be exercised only for the public good’
and not for ulterior and improper purposes.”

[322]

In
Odhavji Estate v. Woodhouse,
2003 SCC 69
at
para.
30
, the Court explained
the rationale
of the tort as “to protect each citizen’s reasonable expectation that a public
officer will not intentionally injure a member of the public through deliberate
and unlawful conduct in the exercise of public functions.”

[323]

For good reason, the ambit
of the tort has always been narrow. As was observed by Madam Justice Newbury
in
Powder Mountain Resorts Ltd. v. British Columbia,
2001 BCCA
619
:

[2]        But for
reasons that are perhaps obvious, the tort must be used cautiously. Otherwise,
the courts risk straying into the arena of political decision-making, bypassing
the normal restraints associated with judicial review, and becoming the
arbiters of the personal thought processes of public officials. One recent
commentator (Phillip Allott, “EC Directives and Misfeasance in Public Office”,
[2000] 59
Camb. L.J.
4) has written that the court should not,
by means of the tort, take on the role of “ombudsman, a parliamentary
committee, or an organ of public opinion in reviewing even egregious acts of
maladministration, official incompetence, or bad judgement.” (at 6.) To avoid
dangers of this kind, a balance must be sought between curbing unlawful
behaviour on the part of governmental officials on the one hand, and on the
other, protecting officials who are charged with making decisions for the
public good, from unmeritorious claims by persons adversely affected by such
decisions. …

[324]

There are two
branches of the tort; both share two common elements: (1) deliberate
unlawful conduct by a public officer in the exercise of his or her powers
(the
actus reus
); and (2) the awareness (knowledge) that the
unlawful conduct is likely to injure the particular plaintiff (the
mens
rea
):

Odhavji
at para. 23. With respect to the
nature of the conduct, “the essential question to be determined is not whether
the officer has unlawfully exercised a power actually possessed, but whether
the alleged misconduct is deliberate and unlawful”:
Odhavji
at
para. 24.

[325]

The two ways this tort can
arise were first described by the House of Lords in
Three Rivers
and
subsequently adopted by the Supreme Court in
Odhavji
:

[22]      …In
Three
Rivers
, the House of Lords held that the tort of misfeasance in a public
office can arise in one of two ways, what I shall call Category A and Category
B. Category A involves conduct that is specifically intended to injure a person
or class of persons. Category B involves a public officer who acts with
knowledge both that she or he has no power to do the act complained of and that
the act is likely to injure the plaintiff.

[326]

Category A misfeasance is
established when a public officer exercises his or her power for the specific
purpose of harming the plaintiff.
Three Rivers
described it as
“targeted malice” that includes conduct done for the ulterior or improper
purpose of harming the plaintiff. Proof of the specific intent to harm the
plaintiff will be sufficient to establish that the public officer had knowledge
his or her conduct was likely to harm the plaintiff:
Odhavji
at
para. 23.

[327]

Category B misfeasance
is more complex. It does not require a finding of specific intent to harm the
plaintiff, but rather
an
objective determination that the public officer knowingly engaged in a
deliberate unlawful act with an awareness that his or her conduct would likely
harm the plaintiff
or a class of plaintiffs.
Knowledge of harm alone is insufficient to establish that the public officer
acted in bad faith or dishonestly. Rather,
the officer must know that the
deliberate conduct is inconsistent with the obligations of the office,
including that it exceeds the powers of the office, or omits a legally required
act
:
Odhavji
at para. 28 and
Powder
Mountain
at para. 67.

[328]

Thus, to establish
Category B misfeasance, the mother was required to prove that
Mr. Strickland deliberately engaged in an unlawful act, knowing of the possible
harmful consequences to her and the children, and she was required to prove
each element of the tort independently of the other:
Odhavji
at
para. 23.

[329]

The mental element of
Category A or Category B misfeasance establishes the “bad faith” or “dishonesty”
of the public officer. Accordingly, it requires “clear proof commensurate with
the seriousness of the wrong”:

Powder
Mountain
at para. 8 and
Odhavji
at
para. 28.
Awareness or knowledge that the unlawful act is likely to
harm the plaintiff requires at least a subjective recklessness or wilful
blindness, if not actual knowledge, of the likely consequences of the unlawful
act:

Powder Mountain
at paras. 7 and
Odhavji
at
paras. 25 and 38. Subjective recklessness or wilful blindness requires a
higher standard of proof than objective foreseeability of harm for negligence.
The mental element of the tort thus constrains its ambit from including
inadvertent or negligent conduct by a public officer in the discharge of his or
her official obligations:
Odhavji
at para. 26.

[330]

In
Powder
Mountain,
Newbury J.A.

addressed this important
distinction as follows:

[7]        …Thus
there remains what in theory at least is a clear line between this tort on the
one hand, and what on the other hand may be called negligent excess of power -
i.e., an act committed without knowledge of (or
subjective
recklessness
as to) its unlawfulness and the probable consequences for the plaintiff. …

[8]        …In
First
National Properties Ltd. v. McMinn
(2001)
2001 BCCA 305 (CanLII)
, 198 D.L.R. (4
th
)
443, we also stated that courts should be cautious in dealing with the tort
because it is an
exception
to the normal disinterest of the
civil law in the motive underlying conduct, as opposed to the conduct itself;
see
Bradford Corp. v. Pickles
(1895) A.C. 587 (H.L.)
. (The
criminal law distinguishes between “motive” and “intention” but that
distinction seems inoperative in the present context.) Motive is of course
notoriously difficult to discern, and one may act for more than one motive.
[Emphasis in original.]

[331]

The policy rationale
behind this narrow application of the tort was also explained in
Odhavji
:

[28]      …In a
democracy, public officers must retain the authority to make decisions that,
where appropriate, are adverse to the interests of certain citizens. Knowledge
of harm is thus an insufficient basis on which to conclude that the defendant
has acted in bad faith or dishonestly. A public officer may in good faith make
a decision that she or he knows to be adverse to the interests of certain
members of the public.
In order for the conduct to fall within the
scope of the tort, the officer must deliberately engage in conduct that he or
she knows to be inconsistent with the obligations of the office.

[Emphasis added
throughout the quote, except for the original emphasis found in paras. 330 and
331.]

[
120
]

As set out above, to prove misfeasance, the plaintiffs must prove
objectively that a public officer knowingly engaged in a deliberate act inconsistent
with their obligations of office with an awareness that his or her conduct
would likely harm the plaintiff.

[
121
]

The ANOCC identifies three individuals who can be considered public
officers for the purposes of this tort: Inspector Ramanzin, Legal counsel
Ohene-Asante and Registrar Johansen. I will consider the tort as against each
of these individuals in turn.

Inspector Ramanzin

[
122
]

It is open on the evidence to find that Ms. Ramanzin investigated
the complaint, attended all Inquiry Committee meetings to present evidence she
gathered and discussed the investigation, and drafted or consulted in the
drafting in whole or in part, of the two consent orders and the Letter of
Expectation.

[
123
]

Inspector Ramanzin argues that aside from conducting the
investigation, all other tasks were performed at the direction of the Inquiry
Committee. She further argues that there is no credible basis to suggest that
she deliberately and knowingly engaged in conduct that was unlawful in the
performance of her duties.

[
124
]

Despite this argument, there is no evidence to prove what if any
tasks the Inspector performed at the direction of the Inquiry Committee. More specifically
there is no evidence regarding what role Inspector Ramanzin played in the
determination of the penalty, ultimate resolution or the decision not to pass
the file on to the Discipline Committee after the Citation was issued.

[
125
]

At this stage my task is to determine whether there is some basis
for the tort applying the skeptical analysis test. I find that the following
facts/ inferences that can be drawn from the evidence provide a credible basis
for a claim of misfeasance against Inspector Ramanzin:

i.

Throughout the investigation Inspector Ramanzin
changed the allegations (date, location and facts) in order to strengthen the
case against Alice instead of questioning the veracity of Ms. Blatta’s
complaint. The versions of the main incident, (which ultimately became the
January 10 incident) changed in material ways at least three times. Further,
Inspector Ramanzin failed to confirm that Ms. Blatta was working on the date
she said she witnessed the first and most serious incident (she was not).

ii.

Based at least in part on Inspector Ramanzin’s submissions to the
members of the Inquiry Committee, the College offered two consent orders as a
means of settling the Complaint. The first was for Alice to agree to give up
her nursing licence with no right to apply for reinstatement for three years.
The second offer made on November 20, 2020, was dramatically less stringent: a
6-month suspension. In the second offer, Inspector Ramanzin set out “facts” materially
different than those set out in the first Consent Order and then presented to
the Inquiry Committee.

iii.

When Alice rejected the Second Consent Order, the Inspector advised
her that the matter would be going for Disciplinary Hearing. The file was never
passed onto the Disciplinary Committee leaving doubt as to the veracity of this
assertion.

iv.

In the December 23, 2020 Inquiry Committee meeting after the matter
had been ongoing for approximately a year and a half, the Inspector advised the
Inquiry Committee that the evidence was not as strong as she had previously
represented.

v.

The Inspector was involved in the decision to “resolve” the matter
through a LOE knowing that Alice vehemently denied the allegations and wanted
to prove her innocence through the disciplinary hearing.

vi.

The LOE that the Inspector drafted included “facts” that the Inspector
knew could not be proved at a hearing and “conclusions” that she knew were not
available on the evidence.

vii.

The Inspector knew or ought to have known that the LOE deprived
Alice of a hearing on its merits and would result in a permanent entry on her
nursing record that would impact her career, thereby causing her harm.

[
126
]

By continually changing the “facts” knowing that they were false in
an attempt to strengthen the complaints against Alice, failing to fully
investigate the complaint and failing to advise the Inquiry Committee as to the
weaknesses in the evidence, Inspector Ramanzin prolonged the inquiry process,
knowing that it was causing Alice mental distress and knowing that it was an
abuse of her duties. Given the above, I am satisfied that there is some basis
for the tort of misfeasance against Inspector Ramanzin that would not be
protected by statutory immunity.

Legal Counsel Ohene-Assante

[
127
]

Although it is not specified in the minutes of the Inquiry Committee
meetings of June 13, 2019 or July 14 2020, I find that it is likely that legal
counsel was present for all Inquiry Committee meetings. She was responsible for
giving legal advice to the Inquiry Committee and to the Inspector. As such, she
was at the very least aware that there were credibility/ reliability issues
with Ms. Blatta’s version of events, and that the facts upon which the Inquiry
Committee was basing its decisions kept changing.

[
128
]

Legal counsel Ohene-Asante made the second offer to settle indicating
that, while she was not the statutory decision maker, she was at the very least
a part of the decision-making team. Given the apparent arbitrariness in the
consent dispositions offered, the fact that she was part of the decision to
dispose of the complaint with a LOE knowing that the “facts” were denied and
likely knowing that the College would have difficulty proving them, and knowing
that the LOE would deprive Alice of her opportunity have the matter decided on
its merits and that the LOE would be a black mark on her employment record for
the rest of her career, I am satisfied that there is some evidentiary basis for
the tort of misfeasance against Ms. Ohene-Assante that would not be protected
by statutory immunity.

Registrar Johansen

[
129
]

Registrar Johansen’s only involvement in the disciplinary process
was issuing and then later cancelling the Citation at the direction of the
Inquiry Committee. In doing so, the Registrar was carrying out her statutory
duties as required under
s. 37
of the
HPA
.
Accordingly,

I find
that Registrar Johansen is protected under the
s. 24(1)
of
HPA.

[
130
]

Registrar Johansen is removed as a defendant pursuant to Rule
6-2(7).

Charter
Breaches

[
131
]

I am not satisfied that any of the alleged breaches of the
Charter

of Rights are supported by the facts or available to the plaintiffs.
Accordingly, each of the
Plaintiffs’ claims for
Charter

damages as
against the BCCNM Defendants should be struck out under Rule 9-5(1)(a).

APPLICATION TO REMOVE PARTIES

George Thmbran

[
132
]

During the hearing the plaintiffs withdrew the loss of spousal
consortium claim conceding that there is no such cause of action in British
Columbia.

[
133
]

While I acknowledge the impact that the disciplinary process has had
(and continues to have) on George, the alleged tortious conduct concerns Alice
only. As none of the defendants owe George a duty of care, he has no action
against any of them.

[
134
]

Accordingly, pursuant to Rule 6-2(7), George is removed as a
plaintiff.

BCCNM Inquiry Committee

[
135
]

The BCCNM defendants seek to have the Inquiry Committee removed as a
party on the basis that it is not a corporate entity distinct from BCCNM and
does not have the legal capacity to be sued in its own right.

[
136
]

On the basis of the evidence before me, I am not prepared to remove
the Inquiry Committee as a party.

APPLICATION TO DISMISS ALL CLAIMS
AGAINST THE PROVINCE

[
137
]

The plaintiffs name as a defendant, the Province, on the basis that
they are vicariously liable having appointed BCCNM Board members and conferred
powers under the
HPA
.

[
138
]

The common law test known as the Salmond test (from Salmond and
Heuston's treatise on torts: see, e.g., Salmond and Heuston on the
Law of Torts (19th ed. 1987), at pp. 521-22) posits that vicarious
liability is imposed on an employer for the conduct of their employees where
the loss against a third party was authorized or sufficiently connected to
conduct authorized by the employer (
Bazley v. Curry
,
1999 CanLII 692 (SCC)
, [1999] 2 SCR 534 at
535). The rationale is to ensure the harmed party has a remedy and to deter
future harm.

[
139
]

The Province appoints two BCCNM board members. It does not exercise
authority over the board or the Inquiry Committee’s conduct. Once appointed,
board members are individually responsible for discharging their duties in
accordance with the
HPA
. In any event, at all material times the College
was acting independently and not as agents of the Province.

[
140
]

Furthermore, imposing vicarious liability upon the Province for the statutory
decisions of every person appointed to a regulatory body would undermine the
important function of delegating authority to administrative bodies to regulate
professional conduct, as well as undermine the executive branch’s authority to
enact statutes like the
HPA
.

[
141
]

I see no viable cause of action and dismiss any and all claims as
against the Province pursuant to Rule 9-5(1)(a).

CONCLUSION

[
142
]

For the reasons above I make these orders:

1.

Pursuant to Rule 6-2(7), George is removed as a plaintiff and
Registrar Johansen and the Province are removed as defendants in this
proceeding. The style of cause shall be amended to remove them as parties;

2.

Pursuant to Rule 9-5(1)(a), the following claims are struck from the
NOCC and ANOCC:

a.

Abuse of Rights

b.

Abuse of Process

c.

Civil Conspiracy

d.

Civil fraud or deceit

e.

All of the
Charter
claims

3.

Pursuant to Rule 9-5(1) the claim of misfeasance is struck as
against Registrar Johansen only;

4.

Pursuant to Rule 9-5(1)(a) the claim against the Province is struck
in its entirety;

5.

I grant leave to the plaintiff to amend the proceedings to bring a
petition for Judicial Review if they so choose. I further grant an extension of
time until May 15, 2024 for the petitioners to do so.

6.

I grant leave to the parties to amend their pleadings to amend the
claim of malicious use of process to a claim of malicious prosecution;

7.

I grant leave to the plaintiffs to amend their pleadings regarding
the claim of defamation to clarify what words they allege as defamatory.

8.

I grant leave to the plaintiff to amend the ANOCC to clarify the
facts relating to each cause of action.

[
143
]

As success is divided between the BCCNM defendants and the
plaintiff, each party shall bear their own costs.
